headline: Android Motion Assist feature aims to cure car sickness
summary: Google is rolling out a new feature that uses on-screen dots to counteract motion sickness, similar to Apple's existing technology.
details: Google is rolling out a new Android feature called Motion Assist, designed to reduce or eliminate motion sickness experienced while using a phone in a moving vehicle. This feature is very similar to Apple's Motion Cues, which was introduced in 2024.

Motion Assist utilizes the device's accelerometer and gyroscope to display dots around the screen's periphery. These dots move in sync with the vehicle's motion, sweeping left when the car turns right and sliding forward when the car brakes, to help mitigate the sensory conflict that causes nausea.

The effectiveness of this technology has been personally verified, with users reporting that it significantly improves their ability to work on devices while traveling. The feature can be configured with adjustable opacity, shape, and color for the motion indicators.

Motion Assist can be set to automatically activate when a moving vehicle is detected or manually toggled via a Quick Settings tile. While not yet available on all devices, it is reportedly rolling out in phases, with some Pixel phones receiving it first.

headline_marked: [[Calculate AI Agent ROI]] Before You Build: A Practical Framework
headline: Calculate AI Agent ROI Before You Build: A Practical Framework
summary: Don't ask 'is AI worth it?' Instead, calculate the break-even point by comparing manual costs to agent build and run expenses.
details: To accurately calculate the ROI of an AI agent, compare the fully-loaded cost of the current manual process (including labor, error correction, and missed volume) against the agent's one-time build cost plus its ongoing per-run inference cost. The key is to solve for the volume at which these costs equalize.

The critical question isn't 'is AI worth it,' but rather, 'does automating this specific task at this volume pay back faster than the cash and attention it costs to build and run?' This framework helps founders avoid costly, unanswerable questions.

Costing out the manual process involves multiplying time-per-unit by monthly volume to get a true status quo cost. This figure, which typically includes error and opportunity costs, is the benchmark the agent must beat.

Agent build costs include scoping, prompt iteration, system integration, and initial monitoring. For a well-scoped, single-purpose agent, this is often manageable within an MVP timeline, not a multi-quarter platform build.

Ongoing run costs per unit cover inference tokens and API calls. These must be derived from real test batches, not spec sheets, to avoid compounding errors with volume. Guessing here is a common pitfall.

Opting for a single, well-designed model call instead of a multi-step agent chain can significantly reduce per-unit run costs and improve output consistency. This architectural choice can accelerate the break-even point.

For example, if manual cost per unit is $4.50 and agent run cost is $0.15, a $6,000 build cost breaks even at approximately 1,380 units. If monthly volume exceeds this, profitability can be achieved within the first month.
Low-volume, highly variable tasks—typically the 20% involving exception handling and heavy judgment—rarely clear break-even and are often cheaper to leave with human operators.

Beyond direct cost savings, AI agents unlock new possibilities. The true ROI often comes from increased volume and quality that human teams cannot achieve at scale, such as personalized outreach at a mass scale.

When scoping ROI, consider what becomes possible at the new cost and speed, not just what gets cheaper. Define clear metrics for success, such as a break-even date or an accuracy floor, before development begins.
